clue.text: Distort emphasis in broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered about, so these letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone warns that stressing the wrong words on air twists the meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' reads as radio, but it signals that EMPHASIS is rearranged; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To distort something is to twist it out of its proper form, which is a synonym.

clue.text: Impudently dispensed paltry meal

indicators.note: dispensed means handed out, so the letters are dealt out in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A canteen cheekily serves up a miserable lunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Malapert is an old word for impudent or saucy, so the adverb means impudently.

clue.text: All one has, with half the season gone

indicators.note: half the means only the front three of its six letters are kept

parts.note: summer is a season

explanation.surface: Someone's whole stock is spent with half the season still to run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half the ... gone' keeps SUM from SUMMER; 'gone' completes the indicator and 'with' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum is a total amount, as in one's whole sum of money, everything one has.

clue.text: Foot-soldier is bound to fire when told

indicators.note: when told means when spoken, so the letters are what the words sound like

parts.note: bound is hop and fire is light, joined by to

explanation.surface: An infantryman is obliged to shoot on command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' looks like 'obliged' and 'fire' like shooting, but they are HOP and LIGHT; 'is' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoplite was a heavily armed infantryman of ancient Greece, a historical type of foot-soldier.

clue.text: One who has voluntarily undergone third degree perhaps?

definitions.text: One who has voluntarily undergone third degree perhaps?

parts.words: One who has voluntarily undergone third degree perhaps?
parts.note: third degree suggests harsh interrogation, but here it is a doctorate following a first and a master's degree

explanation.definitionFit: A student studying beyond a first degree may go on to a doctorate, a third academic qualification.

clue.text: Money that's going to plan

indicators.note: the letters for that's are going to, i.e. joining onto the end of, the plan

parts.note: spec, short for specification, is a detailed plan
i.e. (id est) means that is

explanation.surface: Cash that is about to be spent according to a budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going to' is the charade signal: the 'that's' abbreviation is attached after the plan word. 'Money' can look like part of the surface, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Specie is money in coin rather than notes, a slightly formal synonym.

clue.text: Girl in photograph is unromantic

indicators.note: in puts the girl inside the photograph

parts.note: pic is short for picture or photograph
Rosa is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A woman shown in a snapshot looks thoroughly unglamorous.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosaic means dull and matter-of-fact, the opposite of romantic or poetic.

clue.text: Ditch sermon prepared for all the faithful

indicators.note: prepared means made ready, so the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A preacher is told to scrap the address written for the congregation.
explanation.definitionFit: Christendom means the whole body of Christian believers worldwide.

clue.text: Nordic verses in English supplement turned up

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to add is to supplement

explanation.surface: Scandinavian poems appear in an English-language supplement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' turns ADD into DDA; 'in' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edda is a medieval Icelandic collection of Norse mythological poetry.

clue.text: Standard of urban enlightenment

parts.note: a standard here is an upright post, one that lights up a town street rather than a measure of civic learning

explanation.definitionFit: A street light's upright is called a lamp standard, and it enlightens the town in the literal sense.

clue.text: Stolen staff car

parts.note: hot is slang for stolen goods
a rod is a staff or stick

explanation.surface: A rod taken from the office goes missing along with a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot rod is a car modified for speed, so car is the category it belongs to.

clue.text: Fighting retreat under building, one seen to smoke

indicators.note: in a down clue the fighting and retreat words sit under the building

parts.note: a church is a building
war is fighting
a den is a private retreat

explanation.surface: Troops falling back beneath a structure are spotted through the smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: A churchwarden is also a long clay tobacco pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A churchwarden is a long-stemmed clay pipe, something people smoke.

clue.text: Knocking noises you have to listen to on board clipper

parts.note: pinking is the metallic knocking of a badly tuned engine

indicators.note: being on board a ship puts the listening word inside the ship's letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, the vessel one boards
to hear is to listen to

explanation.surface: A passenger on a sailing clipper complains of banging sounds heard below decks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is the old convention for going inside SS: HEAR sits within SS to give SHEARS; 'you have to' is linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinking shears are zigzag scissors, a tool that clips cloth, so clipper describes them.

clue.text: Cheat upset comrade about spell of duty in the night

indicators.note: about means around, so the cheat and comrade words go round the spell of duty
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: to con is to cheat
an ally is a comrade
a turn is a spell of duty

explanation.surface: A swindler unsettles a colleague during a night shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' suits a down clue, where the cheat word is read bottom to top; 'about' then wraps the cheat and comrade pair round the duty spell.
explanation.definitionFit: Nocturnally means by night or during the hours of darkness, a direct paraphrase.

clue.text: A chap keeping no end of racehorses is sharp

indicators.note: no end of means the final letter is removed

parts.note: a string is the group of racehorses kept by one stable
gent is short for gentleman, a chap

explanation.surface: A man who owns a stable of horses has a sharp edge.
explanation.walkthrough: A string is a trainer's stable of racehorses, a horse-racing usage; 'no end of' drops its last letter before the chap word keeps it.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent describes something sharp or biting, as in astringent criticism.

clue.text: Pity about church gathering

indicators.note: about means around, so the pity word goes round the church letters

parts.note: rue means pity or regret

explanation.surface: Someone regrets what goes on at a congregation's meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruche is a gathered frill of fabric, so gathering in the dressmaking sense names it.

clue.text: Expose warders as pushers

parts.note: to air an opinion or a room is to expose it
screws is prison slang for warders

explanation.surface: A whistleblower reveals prison guards as drug dealers.
explanation.walkthrough: SCREWS is British prison slang for warders.
explanation.definitionFit: An airscrew is a propeller, and a pusher propeller drives an aircraft forward.

clue.text: Pistol, for example, making raucous entrance

parts.note: loud means raucous or noisy
a mouth is an entrance, as of a cave or river

explanation.surface: A gun goes off noisily as someone comes in.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is not a gun but the swaggering braggart in Shakespeare's Henry plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Pistol is a boastful ranter, a classic example of a noisy braggart.

clue.text: A sucker from pots full of drink

indicators.note: full of means the pots hold the drink inside them

parts.note: mugs are drinking pots
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: A gullible person drinks from cups brimming with liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: Muggins is a British jocular word for a fool or dupe, a person easily taken in.

clue.text: Girl left to struggle below

annotationWithheld.why: Girl left to struggle below (5): no parse found giving UNDER from 'Girl left' and an indicator; neither scan nor search shows another reading

clue.text: Relative nipped by snake has to let go

indicators.note: nipped means having the tip bitten off, so the last letter goes

parts.note: an uncle is a relative
an asp is a snake

explanation.surface: A family member bitten by a serpent has to release his grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nipped' suggests a bite, but it means the relative loses his tip; 'has to' only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To unclasp is to release one's hold, which is letting go.

clue.text: 13 says when it's his turn to look out

definitions.text: 13 says when it's his turn to look out

parts.words: 13 says when it's his turn to look out
parts.note: the answer to 13 down gives the time of his shift, and his duty is keeping a lookout

explanation.definitionFit: A guard who patrols after dark keeps watch through the hours of darkness, which the cross-reference names.

clue.text: Take charge of stud

definitions.meaning: to give orders and take charge
a stud or knob, as on a shield

explanation.definitionFit: Boss as a verb means control, and as a noun a raised ornamental knob or stud.

clue.text: Painting outfit used by a bore

parts.note: an oil is an oil painting
a rig is an outfit of clothes or equipment

explanation.surface: A dull person turns up in a paint-spattered outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a tedious person, but it is a borehole being drilled.
explanation.definitionFit: A drilling platform is the equipment a borehole needs, so it is what a bore uses.

clue.text: Have unrealistic picture of one almost moribund isle, perhaps

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: almost means the word is not quite finished, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: moribund means nearly dead

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the island word might be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A dreamer romanticises a dying island community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts DEAD to DEA; 'perhaps' rearranges ISLE into LISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To idealise is to picture something as better than it really is, an idiomatic paraphrase.

clue.text: Sort of box that is cold inside

indicators.note: inside puts the cold letter within the that-is letters

parts.note: C is short for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A container keeps things chilled within it.
explanation.definitionFit: An icebox is a kind of box, so the word can qualify box.

clue.text: Most self-conscious, being seen in flashy establishment

indicators.note: the answer is seen inside the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: The bashful patron feels most awkward when spotted in a glitzy venue.
explanation.definitionFit: Shy means self-conscious, and the superlative form gives the most self-conscious.

clue.text: A peasant involved in the destruction of Sennacherib?

indicators.note: involved means twisted up, so the letters are entangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A farmer plays a part in the downfall of an Assyrian king.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's poem The Destruction of Sennacherib ('The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold') is written in this metre; the question mark marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's poem is the best-known example of verse in this metrical foot, two short syllables then a long.
